This card used to say "the fly brain's agreement rate is 0.025, only slightly above chance; the connectome contributes nothing to playing". That version had a bug: when the brain's input was changed, the previous batch of stimulation was not cleared, so inputs piled up one after another. As a result almost every board fed in was the same input, and the readout learned noise. The other half of the cause was architecture: v1 spread the whole board randomly over sensory neurons, discarding the locality and translation invariance that matter most in Gomoku. The game itself is not affected by this bug (every step rewrites the whole input group; the results of 7 missions and 10 mutants are identical item by item before and after the fix).

html:<b>① 每条线值多少——果蝇脑 + 一层线性读出。</b>对一个候选: html:① What each line is worth — the fly brain + one linear readout layer. For a candidate point, take one line in each of 4 directions (4 cells on each side, each cell = empty / mine / opponent / edge). There are only 14,641 such line patterns, few enough that this 5,563-neuron fly brain runs every one of them: 8 cells × 3 states = 24 channels, each wired to about 61 real sensory neurons, Poisson-driven for 300 ms; spikes of downstream neurons are counted and averaged over 3 random seeds. Not a single synapse in the brain is trained; only one linear readout layer is trained, converting the firing into the line's log value. Move score = the sum of the values of 4 attack lines + λ × 4 defence lines.
html:<b>② 「推理 N 步」也是训练出来的，不是下棋时现算的。</b>数: html:② "Reason N steps" is also trained, not computed during play. Every position in the dataset is labelled with the best move from searching ahead 1–6 and 8 steps; for each N, one readout layer is trained with that as the label. The reasoning steps setting above the board simply selects which one to use — during play there is only model inference: line pattern → the fly brain's firing → this readout layer → the point with the highest move score, with no search at all. You can switch at any time; the move being considered is immediately rethought with the new one. The board shows its thinking: orange circles = the probability the model assigns to each candidate point, numbered ghost stones = its anticipated continuation (the same model plays N moves for both sides in turn). ③ Forbidden moves and wins are judged by the rules engine. After each move, the page reruns that move's line patterns live in the real brain and compares them with the value table — at that point the spike plot, descending neurons and sensory input on the left show the firing of the fly playing Gomoku. ④ The external search (off by default) is the alpha-beta algorithm: it is given the same value table and searches ahead, knowing only the rules and no shape scores. It is much stronger, but that is the algorithm's credit, and the page labels it separately.

html:<b>一篇值得读的批评</b>：Patrick Mineault，<i: html:A critique worth reading: Patrick Mineault, Deconstructing viral fly sims (2026-09-14, neuroai.science). His core objection: most demos do not build a complete sensory-to-motor closed loop, and visual input acts roughly like a random seed; and "a large enough network can learn many things anyway—does it matter that it is a fly?". The strict standard he proposes: behaviour must be genuinely driven by the senses, activity must be electrophysiologically plausible, and it must show individuality.

html:But simply averaging many frames does not help—measured improvement −0.2%, because each measurement is itself a blurred average over ommatidia, and stacking them just averages more blurred images. What actually works is back-projection: solve an inverse problem to find a high-resolution image such that "measuring it with the ommatidia" reproduces all 69,216 measurements. Measured correlation with the original: single frame 0.851 → naive accumulation 0.849 → back-projection 0.920, exceeding the ceiling of 0.883 set by a single acceptance angle —— showing it really recovers information from multiple frames that a single frame does not contain. html:<b>关于颜色</b>：果蝇有色觉，而且比人多一维——R7 是紫外（p: html:About colour: fruit flies have colour vision, with one more dimension than humans — R7 is ultraviolet (pale-type Rh3 ~345 nm / yellow-type Rh4 ~375 nm), R8 is blue (Rh5 ~437 nm) or green (Rh6 ~508 nm), but they can barely see red. html:<b>哪些是手写的：</b>① 触角叶局部神经元一律取抑制性（递质符号: html:What is hand-written: ① all antennal-lobe local neurons are taken as inhibitory (a correction of transmitter sign, supported by the literature); ② edges touching the mushroom body keep only those with ≥2 synapses (the page cannot hold all 1.29 million); ③ the sugar / heat → dopamine wire (the connectome cannot itself activate the dopaminergic neurons, see ②); ④ the three numbers of the plasticity rule (learning rate, eligibility trace 200 ms, no forgetting); ⑤ odour A / B are synthetic (20 glomeruli each), not receptor profiles of real odours; ⑥ the mapping from descending neurons → "step frequency + left/right stride length", and the phase coupling between the six legs — the ventral nerve cord connectome cannot produce a tripod gait (the "Ventral nerve cord" section above); ⑦ the "memory → steering bridge" is entirely hand-written, so it is off by default.

It is not a language model, and the fly cannot talk.

CB0883 is a hub in the whole brain (0.76 knocked out alone, collapsing to 0.24 when paired with Clavicle/G2N-1), and Zorro is a type real experiments confirmed as "required for proboscis extension", yet when either is knocked out alone the fly looks perfectly normal. html:The small window at the top right of the stage is the real-time version of the same thing: the 3D world is rendered again from the position of the fly's eyes (each eye turned 50° towards the front) and imaged through the same sampling table. To run in real time it skips flyvis and the decoder, stopping at "what the retina receives". It used to refresh only 3 times per second, because a synchronous GPU pixel readback waits for a round trip of about 4–5 ms; measurement showed that stall does not depend at all on how many faces are read, how many pixels, or how large the texture is (reading 1 face 6.3 ms ≈ reading 6 faces 6.8 ms; edge length 192→48 is no cheaper), so lowering the resolution does not help. After switching to WebGL2 PBO asynchronous readback (data collected on the next frame, verified byte-identical to the synchronous path), a single read dropped from 10.6 ms to 2.9 ms; it now measures 23 fps, with the main view still at 60 fps.
The "Dodge by eyes only" toggle replaces the game's visual front end: normally the fly reads the ball's world coordinates directly to compute the rate of angular expansion (a hand-written rule that looks only at the ball and ignores everything else in the scene); with it on, the fly can rely only on the readings of these 721 ommatidia — real pixels → Rh1 (R1–R6) → flyvis → T4/T5 pooled away from the centre in the form of Klapoetke et al. 2017 → LC4/LPLC2. The result is negative, and measurable: the ball has a radius of 2.5 mm and the interommatidial angle is 5.7°, so beyond 60 mm the ball covers less than one ommatidium; measured, this real vision is completely blind beyond 45 mm (the reading is constantly 0) and only separates the ball from the noise within 25 mm, whereas the hand-written front end tracks it from 110 mm. Worse, just by walking, the whole-field optic flow of the fly's self-motion creates spurious "looming" peaking at 126 Hz — so with it on the fly scares itself into taking off as it walks. This is not the model being broken; it is the problem that real flies cancel with their antennae and halteres, and this model has neither. The toggle is off by default, and turning it on costs frame rate (about 12 ms each time). During rendering the fly's own mesh is hidden — the camera sits in front of the body, and otherwise its own head would smear across half the field of view.
Each photoreceptor class integrates over its own spectrum: this used to be a Bayer-like approximation ("pale ommatidia take the blue channel, yellow take the green"); now, using the visual-pigment template of Govardovskii et al. 2000, each receptor's weights on the three rendered bands (UV 300–400, blue 400–500, green 500–700) are integrated in 1 nm steps from its own λmax: Rh3 (R7p, 345nm) gets 99.8% from UV, Rh4 (R7y, 375nm) 88.3%, Rh5 (R8p, 437nm) 66.4% blue, Rh6 (R8y, 508nm) 43.4% green. More importantly, Rh1 (R1–R6) has been added — six of the eight photoreceptors, the main channel for motion and brightness, which was previously not modelled at all, and which is precisely flyvis's main input. Two assumptions must be stated: the scene is authored in sRGB with no real spectra, so the three channels are treated as the mean reflectance of each band; and fly R1–6 also have a 3-hydroxyretinol sensitising pigment that gives a second peak at ~350nm, which is not in the template, so it is added here with a hand-picked amplitude (both sets of weights are in results/vision/opsin_weights.json for comparison).
The edge of the visual field is no longer approximate: at first we used perspective projection + FlyGym's fisheye correction, but perspective projection inherently cannot reach 180°; at 157° the edge was already stretched extremely flat, and the fisheye formula also has a singularity. It now uses a cube map — six 90° faces covering the whole sphere, with each ommatidium sampled exactly along its own line of sight, needing no distortion compensation. Ommatidial directions are defined on a hexagonal lattice: radius 15, interommatidial angle 5.7°, 171° field of view per eye, close to the real fly (literature ~160–180°). Measured in a geometry self-check: mean error 0.7° over 9 known directions.
The ultraviolet (R7) channel is a hand-written setting: there is no UV in an sRGB render, so each class of object in the scene was assigned a UV reflectance. The basis is the real structure of the UV world — in nature the sky is by far the dominant UV source and most surfaces are very dark in UV, and flies use exactly this contrast to find open space and tell up from down. But the values have no measured basis at all; they are only structurally plausible, and uploaded photos contain no UV information whatsoever.
Why it looks all green: at first the whole court used the page's theme colour (floor #1a211e), where the green and blue channels differ by only 11%, so to the fly's eye there was effectively no colour; on top of that, each ommatidium measures only one channel and the image is coloured by receptor type, and 70% are the yellow type → 70% of the cells are inherently green. The court now uses realistic colours (wooden floor, white lines, blue and red seats) and applies demosaicing — filling in each ommatidium's missing channel with the average of neighbours of the other type, the same thing a Bayer filter does (the fly itself does not get both channels at every ommatidium; this is interpolation for display, and can be switched off to see the raw mosaic).
Measured after the change: scene G/B went from 36.6/32.5 to 76/49, in-eye G/B = 0.310/0.205, and 41 ommatidia lean blue (the blue seats). But overall it is still greenish, and that is correct — the wooden floor is orange, and the fly has no red receptor, so orange stimulates only its green channel and barely touches the blue one. To a fly, the basketball court is a sheet of dark green.
Still approximate: the interommatidial angle is a constant 5.7° (in real flies it varies from ~4.5° at the front to ~8° at the side); the sky is the game's CSS gradient and not in the 3D scene, so the off-screen render fills the background with the stage sky colour.

html:<b>这就是那条原则的完整答案</b>：只给物理量、不写判断逻辑<b>: html:This is the full answer to that principle: giving only physical quantities without writing decision logic is feasible — once touch is delivered to the head bristles, the number of cells the fly visits rises from 9 to 31.5 and the distance travelled from 156 mm to 603 mm, with no decision of ours in between. But the precondition is that the pathway actually exists in the sub-circuit; delivering it to the wrong place (JO) is the same as giving nothing. The game page still runs v2 + that hand-written "can see the fence", because switching to v3 would require remeasuring all published missions, mutants and knockout ratios — an engineering trade-off, not a scientific conclusion.

html:<b>那为什么不用摄像机？</b>——那条路本来就有：<code>ey: html:So why not use a camera? — That path already exists: eyecam uses a cube-map camera to render the whole 3D scene from the fly's head, with walls, stands and other flies all included, and any object added to the court later will be included automatically. The new horizontal bar in the compound-eye window at top left is its raw projection (before it is sampled into 721 ommatidia). Measured: it does see the wall (reads a constant 0 when still, and responds as soon as it walks), but "walking towards the wall" (LPLC2 median 34.2 Hz) and "walking away from the wall" (23.5 Hz) are barely distinguishable — what it reads is mainly the whole-field optic flow caused by walking itself. Real flies have halteres and efference copies to cancel self-motion; this model has neither.
html:<b>那就只给它物理量，让它自己决定。</b>这是最干净的做法，我们试: html:Then give it only physical quantities and let it decide. That is the cleanest approach, and we tried it: antennae touching the fence → drive mechanosensory neurons. The result: the fly did not react at all (the wall-hugging rate did not move by a single percentage point). The reason is in the connectome: the only mechanosensation in the game's sub-circuit is the antennal JO, and JO connects only to the grooming command aDN1, not to steering or escape at all.

html:<span class=\"tag c\">连接组 · 半</span: html:Connectome · halfThe "what is the fly thinking" bubble: the quantities that trigger each word are real — sweet / bitter / wind / itch are the current frequencies injected into those sensory neurons, and eat / groom / back up / fly are the smoothed firing rates of the readout neurons; but the word thresholds and the Chinese sentence templates are hand-written. This is a simplified version of section 13 of the report: there, 121,706 neurons + ridge regression decode 12 words; here the sub-circuit has only 4,599 neurons and none of the vinegar / mould / temperature and humidity pathways, so it can only use the few inputs that really exist in the game, with thresholds instead of regression.

html:Connectome · halfWind: the game's JO input group is exactly the JO-C/E subtypes — wind / gravity-sensing neurons (Yorozu et al. 2009), and exactly the group that corresponds to "wind" in the "fly speaks Chinese" experiment. So the chain "wind → these neurons fire → downstream readout" is computed by the connectome; the conversion from wind speed to firing frequency, the geometry of the antennae facing the wind, and the force with which the wind pushes the fly off course are all hand-written (there is no calibration data for this model).
html:<span class=\"tag c\">连接组</span><b>: html:connectomeKnock out real neurons: this row of switches are real neurons picked by the virtual knockout screen (report §14–24, 24,250 whole-brain simulation segments), not functional groups. Cutting their outgoing synapses uses the same semantics as the whole-brain screen. The two numbers on each switch are the same neuron's ratio in the sugar pathway and in the water pathway, measured in this sub-circuit (node dodge/measure_neurons.js: pellet pinned 1.3 mm in front of the head in continuous contact → taste neurons at 200 Hz, 3 seeds, mean over the last 1.25 s of 2.5 s); hover to see the whole-brain value (python dodge/measure_neurons_fullbrain.py, 138,639 neurons, same joint knockout + null-median normalization + 6 realizations). But it must be said clearly: this sub-circuit has only 4,599 neurons (3% of the whole brain), so individual neurons can be noticeably distorted. The biggest difference is CB0883—in the whole brain it is a hub ("0.76 knocked out alone, collapsing to 0.24 only when paired with Clavicle/G2N-1"), but in the sub-circuit it has no effect at all (sugar ×1.07, water ×1.00), and pairing is merely additive, because the bypass routes it depends on were cut during pruning. Conversely, Clavicle + G2N-1 is still synergistic in the sub-circuit (0.91 / 0.67 each, 0.50 together, 0.61 expected if independent). Most worth looking at is the contrast between sugar and water: Clavicle barely affects sugar (×0.91) but zeroes water (×0.01); CB0051 likewise (×0.80 / ×0.02); G2N-1 conversely only matters for sugar (×0.67 / ×1.07); Phantom is inhibitory, and knocking it out actually doubles MN9 in the water pathway (×2.06). This is what the conclusion of report §21 looks like in the game—the same proboscis extension, driven by two different sets of wiring. Comparing these 10 neurons' ratios in the whole brain and the sub-circuit as a whole [exploratory, n = 10]: sugar Pearson +0.75, water +0.89—overall the sub-circuit reproduces the whole-brain knockout pattern, somewhat more closely on the water side. The most striking row is still Phantom: knock it out and whole-brain water-pathway MN9 becomes 3.02×, sub-circuit 2.06×—direction and magnitude both match. (This cell previously said "sugar +0.21, water +0.92, the sub-circuit reproduces only the water pathway", which was wrong: sugar used un-normalized values and only the 6 named types; with a unified protocol and all 10 neurons, sugar rises to +0.75.)
html:<span class=\"tag c\">连接组</span>“左侧: html:ConnectomeThe pattern "threat on the left → right DNa active, left giant fibre stronger" is computed by the connection weights themselves, and the same holds in the whole-brain model.
html:<span class=\"tag c\">连接组</span>当前子: html:ConnectomeThe current sub-circuit has 4,599 neurons and 338,837 connections: all paths of at most 3 hops with ≥ 3 synapses between LC4/LPLC2/LC16/sugar/bitter/JO and DNa01, DNa02, the giant fibre, MN9, aDN1 and MDN (chosen from 3 candidate sets by the pre-set rule "≤ 6 MB, ≥ 3× real time, smallest mean deviation"). Neuron parameters are the same as in the Shiu et al. 2024 whole-brain model, dt = 0.1 ms, computed step by step in your browser.
html:<span class=\"tag h\">手写 · 有文献依据</s: html:Hand-written · literature-basedVisual front end (default): following Ache et al. 2019 Curr Biol, LC4 encodes angular velocity and LPLC2 encodes angular size. The functional form comes from the literature; the parameters are hand-picked: LC4 = 0.5 Hz/(°/s), LPLC2 = 200 Hz × Gaussian (centre 45°, width 15°). The original parameters could not be obtained. You can switch back to the first version (both use dθ/dt).
html:<span class=\"tag h\">手写 · 非连接组</sp: html:hand-written · not connectome"Follow the scent" (off by default): pellets emit a Gaussian scent field (σ = 15 mm); the left and right antennae each sample the concentration, and when concentration > 0.01 the fly turns towards the higher side at 120°/s, added on top of DNa steering; pellets already tasted no longer attract. In the whole-brain model a one-sided odour stimulus gives no steering signal, so this step is entirely hand-written; whether it eats after touching a pellet is still decided by the connectome's sugar/bitter → MN9.
html:<span class=\"tag h\">手写</span><b>阳: html:Hand-writtenSunlight: only adjusts the visual front-end gain by a hand-written rule (dark → low contrast → weaker looming detection, down to a minimum of 35%) and the brightness of the picture. Directly stimulating photoreceptors cannot drive descending neurons in this LIF model (measured), so we do not pretend brightness is computed by the connectome.
html:<span class=\"tag h\">手写</span>运动映射: html:Hand-writtenMotor mapping: turning angular velocity = 6°/s × (left DNa − right DNa), based on Rayshubskiy et al.'s description of DNa02 (turns towards the more active side); left/right follow the soma side in the FlyWire annotations. Takeoff when the giant fibre's 20 ms smoothed firing rate exceeds 90 Hz.
html:<span class=\"tag h\">手写</span>进食/梳: html:Hand-writtenFeeding/grooming/backing up: pellet under the head → sugar/bitter 200 Hz; dust on an antenna → that side's JO 200 Hz; LC16 = 0.5 Hz/(°/s) × angular velocity; thresholds MN9 30 Hz, aDN1 20 Hz, MDN 20 Hz; priority takeoff > backing up > feeding > grooming > walking. Proboscis extension is a purely visual rotation of the proboscis mesh; the grooming pose is generated by inverse kinematics bringing the foreleg tips to the antennae (after the foreleg grooming type in the flybody grooming pose dataset).
html:<span class=\"tag h\">显示</span>行走腿部: html:DisplayThe walking leg motion is a looped 25 Hz gait cycle recorded from a FlyGym physics simulation; the fly model is displayed at 2× scale, but collisions are still computed at real size (body radius 1.4 mm, ball radius 2.5 mm).
html:<span class=\"tag h\">真实数据 · 训练好的控制: html:Real data · trained controller · hand-written transitionsFlight is performed in a MuJoCo physics simulation by the trained flight controller published with the flybody paper (Vaxenburg et al. 2025 Nature, figshare trained-fly-policies/flight): the controller follows recordings of real fruit-fly escape flights (Muijres et al. 2014 Science, raw trajectories only), and the body position and attitude are simulation results. Median tracking error is about 0.3 mm and body orientation about 4–6°; the left-turn clip diverges to 7 mm in its last ~30 ms. The wings beat according to the controller's actual output: the controller sets the wingbeat frequency (about 219–221 Hz) and adds a correction force to each joint of the left and right wings; the real wing angles are computed by the physics engine, so left and right are no longer perfectly synchronised (left–right correlation of roll angle 0.52–0.59). Takeoff and landing are still hand-written transitions (takeoff rises 5 mm in 20 ms; after the flight, a 50 ms linear descent): no publicly downloadable fruit-fly takeoff kinematics were found, and the Card lab's FlyPEZ takeoff tracking data are available only on request from the authors. Takeoff direction is set away from the threat following Card & Dickinson 2008: a threat on the left selects the right-turn trajectory. Flight is not controlled by the connectome.

html:「生活」模式的果蝇现在用子回路 v5（<span id=\"lnN\": html:The fly in "Life" mode now uses sub-circuit v5 () = v4 + the connectome's mushroom-body learning circuit: olfactory receptor neurons → projection neurons → Kenyon cells → mushroom-body output neurons (MBONs), plus dopaminergic neurons (PAM, PPL1) and the global inhibitory APL. All wiring comes from FlyWire; the only thing that changes is the Kenyon cell → MBON synapse layer: if a Kenyon cell has just fired and there is dopamine in the same compartment, that synapse is depressed (the site and rule of fruit-fly olfactory memory in the literature: Hige 2015; Cohn 2015; Handler 2019). Which dopaminergic neuron governs which compartment is determined by the DAN → MBON synapse counts in the connectome; we did not write a lookup table. Every table below is measured, and every criterion was written before the run. html:几点必须说明：<b>苦味「没有落点」是对的</b>——它是抑制性的，单: html:A few things must be explained: it is correct that bitter "has no landing point"—it is inhibitory, so on its own it should not drive anything; its role is to suppress sugar-driven MN9 (paper Fig 3B–C, which we reproduced: under the strongest sugar, bitter suppresses 82.4%). Humidity genuinely has no landing point—no strength of drive moves any motor output. Temperature only has one above 400 Hz, which at reasonable stimulus strengths means none. Touch has one at 100–200 Hz, which is why it lets the fly get around the fence. One more interesting point: touch given to both sides at once is actually weaker (at 200 Hz all six readouts are 0)—symmetric left-right drive cancels the left-right difference that steering needs. This is not a bug; it is how the circuit is.

Physics uses real units: gravity 9,810 mm/s²; berries fall from branches, bounce along the terrain normal, roll downhill and ferment once they settle; stones are impenetrable; walking uphill is slower; the sun heats dark slabs; hollows fill with rain and evaporate in sunshine; wind carries scent downwind. The threat changed from "flying balls" to "crawling beetles": at the millimetre scale, a 60 mm/s projectile hits the ground in 0.1 s and stops after rolling a few millimetres, so a ball slowly rolling towards you is not physical.

Both hypotheses were fixed before looking at results, and neither survived. The first: “the more concentrated the pathway, the better wiring predicts single-knockout effects” — it seemed to hold on the sugar and water pathways (“firing rate × 1–3-hop paths”: water {0}, sugar {1}, and water is indeed more concentrated), but flipped once the third pathway, JON, was added (see the previous table: JON is the most concentrated yet least predictable from wiring). Direct synapse counts onto MN9, however, are useless on both pathways (the strongest-effect neurons have not a single direct synapse onto MN9). The falsified one: “backing each other up = taking separate paths”. The correlation between path overlap and pairing outcome is only {2} and {3}, and it is not a degenerate metric (maximum overlap reaches 0.59 / 0.70, and more than half of the pairs have non-zero overlap). Switching to a “dynamic fingerprint” (which whole-brain neurons changed after the knockout; this data is already on disk) is an order of magnitude better and in the pre-registered direction, but after controlling for “perturbation magnitude” only a little remains — and the fingerprint itself is the whole-brain simulation of knocking out each neuron alone. Conclusion: single-knockout effects can be roughly screened with wiring, but “will knocking out two together collapse it” — exactly the part single knockouts cannot see — cannot skip the paired simulation.

In the full ventral nerve cord the rhythm window is narrow: at I = 250 nothing moves, at I = 350 12 of 16 replicates oscillate (8–11.5 Hz), at I ≥ 400 most run away; MDN at both strengths runs away 16/16. The rhythm appears in the motor neurons of all 6 legs (right hind leg oscillates in 75% of replicates under the main condition), but the inter-leg phases are not a tripod gait: ipsilateral middle and hind legs are almost in phase, with only 1–6 samples per pair; the swing and stance modules of the same leg are in phase (+0.94). Driving the body, only the right hind leg swings steadily at 9–10 Hz (0.6–0.7 mm, about 60–70% of the CPG); the other legs swing ≤ 0.07 mm (body vibration); during runaway all 6 legs thrash about wildly with no rhythm. Conclusion: one more rhythmic leg than the front-leg network, but still no gait.

Tracing it: {1}the four types with motor landing points (MBON12 / 26 / 27 / 35) fire not a single spike; the APL inhibition they receive is 2–7 times the Kenyon cell excitation. In real flies APL does not spike and provides local inhibition via graded potentials; this model treats it as an ordinary spiking neuron, and it fires pinned at the refractory limit. After cutting APL → MBON, the responsive MBONs increase to {2} types, and the memory does reach some descending neurons (exploratory: the strongest is {3}), but not those five, so the criterion still fails — as agreed in advance, this cut is not adopted, and we will not modify the model further to fit the behaviour. So the “memory → steering bridge” on the page is hand-written and off by default.

第一次跑时我们取了注释表里全部 1,091 个 JO- 神经元，刺激比论文强得多: On the first run we took all 1,091 JO- neurons in the annotation table, a much stronger stimulus than the paper's (aDN1 baseline {0} Hz vs the paper's 23.3 Hz),

On the first run we took all 1,091 JO- neurons in the annotation table, with stimulation far stronger than the paper's (aDN1 baseline {0} Hz, paper 23.3 Hz), and called only 1 required versus the paper's 6. We later reverse-engineered the paper's stimulus list from its own supplementary table — stimulated neurons fire at exactly the stimulus frequency (20 Hz column ≈ 20, 200 ≈ 200) — and the 146 neurons picked out this way match the union of the three subsets in the notebook exactly. Redoing the whole pathway with this list ({1} in the model, 160 Hz): baseline {2} Hz (paper 23.3), Pearson {3}, {4} / {5} of the paper's required neurons called, and κ rises from {6} to {7}. The jump in κ is worth a separate look: under both stimuli the “call agreement” is above 98%, only because 274 of 280 neurons are called “not required” by both sides; remove that luck and the original model barely reproduced the paper's calls at all — on such extremely imbalanced calling problems agreement is misleading, you have to look at κ. But κ has its own trap: the sugar pathway at 100 Hz has κ = 1.00, which looks perfect, but only because MN9 saturates and each side calls just 2 required neurons — with too few positives κ is just as unreliable. The informative sugar condition is 50 Hz, and the table uses its null-normalized 0.59 — the same protocol as the water and JON columns (un-normalized it is 0.63). The conclusion is unchanged and cleaner: of {8} active neurons only aBN1's knockout drives aDN1 to zero (ours 0.00, paper 0.00, and it is exactly the one Hampel et al. 2015 found required for grooming experimentally); 0 of 66 double-knockout pairs are synergistic, and the largest Δ is only +0.07. After knocking out all 596 active neurons one by one (1,319 extra segments), we also got a result opposite to the pre-registered one: JON is the most concentrated of the three pathways (Gini 0.922, tied with water's 0.921), yet the least predictable from wiring alone (G3 0.288, lower even than sugar's 0.316). The pre-registered direction was “more concentrated → wiring predicts better”, and it does not hold across three pathways — recorded here honestly. Each pathway has its own shape: sugar = distributed with a backup network (n80 = 62), water = a few neurons each carrying part and heavily synergistic (n80 = 15), JON = one absolute bottleneck + a large set of nearly irrelevant neurons (only 5 required, but 44 still needed to carry 80% of the effect). (* The JON cell originally read “2 / 2”, which was wrong: Hampel et al. 2015 validated two neurons, aBN1 and aBN2, but aBN2's v630 ID no longer exists in the v783 connectome, so we could not test it at all; and in the paper's own Table 7D the same ID has a ratio of 0.844, which is not called required at the 0.8 threshold. The only one we can test is aBN1, and we called it correctly.) (The JON column has been re-run with the paper's stimulus list and all {9} active neurons, on exactly the same protocol as the sugar / water columns.)

Entering via the leg nerves are 394 chordotonal neurons, 78 hair plates and 9 campaniform sensilla. Version 1, "tonic encoding" (firing by joint angle): the chordotonal neurons fire constantly at a mean of 8 Hz, pushing the network into runaway (237–274 active motor neurons); the original right hind leg rhythm disappeared, and correct and mismatched mappings gave the same result. Version 2, "phasic encoding" (firing by direction only while a joint moves, 0 at rest): receptors fire only 1–6% of the time; at 16 Hz the correct mapping kept the rhythm in 3/3 (version 1: 0/3), but still only the right hind leg was rhythmic, with no inter-leg coordination; the mismatched mapping ran away in 1/3 and in 1/3 gained an extra right middle leg, with no consistent difference from the correct mapping; at 50 Hz it ran away again. Conclusion: phasic encoding no longer destroys the rhythm, but the feedback does not bring out a gait either. The body is fixed with no ground load and the other legs barely move — a clear limitation.
